valuesOpenTreatment_3: If you see a patient and they are not compliant with your management plan, then your appointment with them was almost pointless. You need to consider the patient's situation and before forming a management plan, you have to make sure that the patient is willing to participate/comply with it, given their circumstance.
manipCheckOpen_T: This survey is about the relationships that providers have with their patients and how this relationship lays an important role in the management of patient's medical conditions.
sayingTreatment: Remember that when you see patients, they will be presenting for a number of reasons. Some patients have an acute issue. Some patients are there for chronic conditions. Some patients may be seen for prevention. When you see a patient, you need to take their entire circumstance into consideration. You as the healthcare provider may not initially have all the answers about a person's medical condition after seeing that patient just one time. Try to promote continuity of care with patients and help guide them to help them with their subjective complaints but also guide them through health conditions that they don't necessarily "feel," like high cholesterol. I have found myself throughout the years having to explain to patients, I know you are coming in because you feel "x, y and z" and we will do our best to address those issues. However, you also have other medical conditions that you may not necessary "feel" and these conditions possibly could lead to a number of complications in the future if they are not addressed. Be cautious not just to look at lab results and studies. Listen to your patients. They often may give you clues about what their diagnosis is or how they can be better managed from what they tell you.
ypTreatment3_1:
One thing I look at is if a patient is "self pay." I know many other providers I work with don't always pay attention to the patient's health insurance. If I know the patient is paying for the full cost of the medication out of pocket, I will often look up the medication I want to prescribe them on a website like GoodRx. I'll even print the coupon from the website for them and tell them I recommend a certain pharmacy to dispense it because the cost is cheaper there. Obviously, I confirm with the patient that this is the pharmacy they want the script to go to before sending it in.

When there are choices involved in a management plan, I try to explain the different options to the patient using an "RBA" format. If you are unfamiliar with this acronym, it means "risk, benefit, alternative"... I present the various options and go over the "RBA" of each one. That way the patient can make an informed decision about what they want to do. With more complex management, sometimes the patient needs longer to think about the various options and in non-acute situations, I encourage a patient to think it over and they do not need to make an immediate decision right there at the time of the encounter.
ypTreatment4: When seeing patients with acute issues like a cold (upper respiratory infection) or diarrhea (often a viral gastroenteritis), there is often an attitude from the patient of "doctor, you need to do something." The patient is not feeling well, the patient has a number of life events coming up and they "can't afford" to be ill. The patient's feeling is that the provider needs to prescribe them something so they can get better right away or "nip it in the bud and stop it from getting worse." The quickest way out of the exam room is to just write a prescription for that patient and send them on their way because you basically satisfied their rationale for wanting to come for an appointment that day. It takes more time and use of skills to explain to the patient "that's not the way it works." Most viral illnesses do not have specific medications that "cure" the illness. In most cases, the illness just needs to run its course, and that person needs to relax and let their body do the work to help them get over their illness. There may be some medication that may be prescribed to help alleviate some of the symptoms, but these medications do nothing to make the illness go away any faster or "stop it from getting worse."

valuesOpenTreatment_3: I have always tried to get to know who my patients are, as individuals.  I want to have their trust.  I will make suggestions on what they should do to change/improve their lives.  They must feel seen and known first. I cannot afford to blow them off, even if they are a bit different.  I learn more about myself through this process too, and can have very different relationships with all kinds of people.

But suggesting tiny, micro-steps in weight loss and exercise, while chatting about his work, he began to incorporate those tiny things into his day. sayingTreatment:
Dear New Practitioner,

You are about to begin a new and challenging phase of you life.  Hopefully you have learned the science and medical teaching well.  Now comes the time when you must interface with individual people of this world.  Each one is unique and has a valuable perspective.  They are usually open to learning from you, given your position.  If I could recommend ideas to you, I'd recommend proposing changes, not imposing them.  These are not your serfs.  They are independent, often talented, people who see things not the way you do.  Propose suggestions.  Offer choices, so they can pick what they are able to do.  If you offer, and don't force, you may be better heard.  

Always offer hope.  Offer people a few different ideas.  Try to keep a "next step" in you back pocket.  When I am out of ideas, then I suggest a specialist.  But I tell them I will stay with them through the process.  I suggest you offer to be their guide, their backstop, the one always in their camp.  I think this approach  may help you bond with patients and give them the choice to be loyal to you.  Sadly, that is rare today, as everyone seems to kick the can down the road.  Be the one who stops the buck with you.

Enjoy people.  Rejoice when you help people reach their goal.  You will get satisfaction and you will help people.

sayingTreatment: You are beginning and exciting, exhausting journey. sayingTreatment: Patient care can be challenging, frustrating, and disheartening in so many ways, but please continue to see these patients as fellow human beings, like one of your loved ones (eg: your father, your mother, your grandparent, your child). Taking the time to listen to your patient, collaborate with them, and advocate for them through education and empathy is worthwhile and makes the job doable and sustainable. Remember that each person has such a different life history that forms whom they now are, and try to enter your interactions with that open-mind and openheart, with less judgment.
ypTreatment3_1: I try to ask open-ended questions and practice active listening. It's important to listen and take the time to get the patient's perspective and get to the root of what the patient is wanting to ask, even when it's sometimes difficult for them to say it outright.
ypTreatment4:
I have had many instances where patients have started the conversations very anxious, with rushed speech, and many gripes. With some patient listening and asking nonjudgmental and empathetic questions, they have sometimes shown de-escalation with slower and calmer speech. This doesn't always happen, but it's so rewarding when I've seen how helpful it's been for the patient. I've had patients who were disillusioned with traditional medicine tell me that they have faith in the medical profession again. 
It doesn't even always take a lot of time. Sometimes I've found that just quietly and actively listening result in shorter and more fulfilling visits. When I've tried 'shutting things down' quicker, it feels like we both get escalated, and the visit can sometimes last a lot longer.

sayingTreatment: Remember that the majority of people do not seek medical care, and those who do typically do so when they are feeling weak, sick, and vulnerable. When you are feeling at your worst, literally entrusting your health and life with a potential stranger, it can be intimidating and scary to turn over that control to a physician. And ultimately we are not the ones going home with the patients to ensure they heed our advice or follow our recommendations. And if they don’t like us, why would they do what we say? sayingTreatment: Congratulations! Starting out as a new attending can be overwhelming. You will feel like you have jumped into the deep end and are furiously treading water trying to juggle patient visits, paperwork, messages and your home life. valuesOpenTreatment_3: Being a physician and an underrepresented minority, I understand how important it is to be sensitive to people of different backgrounds.  I wish I had the time describe the number of complaints have had of other physicians who did not take into account their background.
ypTreatment1_1: Understanding a patient's background is very important to explaining why they do certain things. For instance, in Hispanic culture, when a musculoskeletal injury occurs, they usually seek out a "sobador." This is a person who massages the injury to decrease the swelling and reset the ligaments and tendons. Unfortunately, if the patient has a fracture, the "sobador" is actually going to do more damage than good.  This is when non-Hispanic physicians do not understand why did they seek alternative therapy before coming to them first.
ypTreatment1_2: In the example provided in the prior question, if physicians understand that Hispanic patients will seek out a "sobador" first, this would prevent further questioning of the patient and possible shame.
ypTreatment2_1: Knowledge is a significant factor in why patients won't ask questions. Some don't want to understand the disease but rather just accept the instructions on how to control their medical conditions.  This is why speaking their language and knowing their customs will make them trust the physician.  With trust comes the courage to ask questions.
ypTreatment2_1.1: I had a thirty-year-old Hispanic female who was an elementary school teacher and had transferred care to me because her diabetes mellitus type 2 was out of control.  Her hemoglobin A1c upon transfer was over 10.0.  I understood this individual was intelligent, but nothing had ever been explained to her regarding her disease or medications.  Thus, I decided to spend over 30 minutes explaining to her how to use the medications and possible side effects.  She became her own boss once she understood how the medications worked and what a hemoglobin A1c measured.  She was able to lower her hemoglobin A1c to less than 7.0, and I had to decrease the dosages of the medications because she finally had an understanding of the disease and medications.  If a college-educated woman was not able to understand her disease process because nobody took the time to explain it, imagine how a person with an elementary school education is going to feel.

sayingTreatment: Time constraints are a big hurdle in the practice of medicine.  Our goal as providers is always to stay on schedule, even though this might come at the expense of our patients.  I advise you to forget about the schedule and focus your attention on the patients.  Some patients will require longer than 15-20 minute office visits.  Do not be discouraged and put in the time for the patient.  They will realize how vital patient care is to you and will start to develop trust with you.  Once you invest that time with the patient, the follow-up visits will be much smoother and will not take as long.  Many of these patients want someone to listen to them—best of luck. I am here if you require assistance.

sayingTreatment:
I hope this message finds you well. I am writing to discuss an important aspect of our healthcare delivery that I believe can significantly enhance patient outcomes and satisfaction: prioritizing patient perspectives and meeting them where they are.
In our practice, we have observed that engaging patients in their care decisions and understanding their unique circumstances can lead to better adherence to treatment plans and overall improved health outcomes. Here are a few strategies we have found effective:
 Active Listening and Empathy: Taking the time to listen to patients' concerns and experiences without interruption helps build trust and rapport. Empathy in our interactions can make patients feel valued and understood.
 Shared Decision-Making: Involving patients in the decision-making process regarding their treatment options ensures that their values and preferences are considered. commitment to the chosen plan.
 Cultural Competence: Understanding and respecting the cultural backgrounds and beliefs of our patients can help tailor our communication and care plans to be more effective and respectful.
 Flexible Care Plans: Recognizing that each patient’s situation is unique, we should be prepared to adapt care plans to meet their specific needs and circumstances. This might include considering their social determinants of health, such as access to transportation, financial constraints, and family support systems.
 Patient Education: Providing clear and accessible information about their conditions and treatment options empowers patients to make informed decisions. Utilizing various educational tools and resources can cater to different learning preferences.
I believe that by incorporating these strategies into our practice, we can create a more patient-centered approach that not only meets patients where they are but also fosters a more positive and effective healthcare experience.
I look forward to discussing this further and exploring ways we can collaborate to enhance our patient care practices.
Best regards,

ypControl1: Over the years, patients not showing up for appointments has been very, very frustrating, especially after implementing a system of having them called the day before with reminders.  I now wonder if email reminders would be more useful.  I address noncompliance with medications by trying to help patients find a support system.  I have enough education from Alanon and life experience to know that I can not control what anyone does 5 seconds after they leave my presence!  People like diabetics I try to get involved in ongoing support programs like overeaters anonymous where they will have support and their stresses addressed.  I do not have comparable success getting people to exercise.
ypControl2a: With the advent of problems like fentanyl, I have experienced a great deal of sadness because of the extremely high mortality rate in young people.  I am sad also when people do not follow any of my recommendations regarding diabetic care and begin to experience the complications.  Unlike fentanyl with sudden death, diabetics have worse and worse complications and do not die and it is frustrating to see people develop major complications because of nonadherence and then start to adhere to recommendations when the complications have already occurred.  It is kind of like trying to close the barn door after the cow has been gone for several months.

sayingControl: Hi!  The world has gotten smaller.  We can communicate in real time visibly and audibly over great distances.  I have been able to remotely attend the annual American College of Physicians meetings and the content of the meeting is kept active for the month afterward instead of just the three days of the Conference.  In May, I was able to attend 48 hours of Continuing Medical Education at my own pace and my leisure without time lost to travel.  I was also able to pace it so that I did not become oversaturated and fail to be able to retain the material.  A major added benefit has been to not have to get up at 4 a.m. PST to attend a 7 a.m. lecture on the East Coast since fatigue is a major contributor of burnout.  Prescribing software which I initially thought to be another nuisance has become a reliable tool especially since it automatically notes medication interactions.  I have spoken at meetings in Warsaw, Poland,  London, and Perth Australia without needing to travel and without any jet lag!  I communicate on a weekly basis with my grandchildren in another country and enjoy staying connected with their lives.

sayingTreatment: Medicine today is full of distractions and time consuming procedures that detract from patient and physician satisfaction.  Some of them will always be out of your control.  Because of that fact, it is critical that you focus on what you can control.  Your individual relationships with your patients, whether as a long-time primary care physician or the cardiologist saving their life or the surgeon fixing what ails them, can mean everything to the patient.  Showing them empathy and meeting them in their current circumstances without any judgement can empower them to make healthy choices.  Being invested in them, not just their diagnoses, help them remember they are important.  And by investing the time to get to know your patients, you remind yourself that we aren't treating random numbers, but instead patients with families and challenges and gifts.  That humanity is often lost in healthcare and it is our responsibility to recognize that.
ypTreatment3_1:
As a private practice owner, I give patients my time.  New patient appointments are always booked in 90 minute slots and my shortest follow up appointment is 30 minutes.  I don't want my patients to feel rushed or unheard.  My waiting room has a coffee "bar" that all patients are welcome to use, as well as hot and cold water.  I also keep snacks in my office for patients or their children who need to eat.  I keep various activities such as puzzles, coloring books, stickers, etc that patients and kids can use while they wait, most of which they are free to take with them when they leave.  I have a large "community puzzle" that anyone is free to work on at any time.  My patient bathroom has diapers, wipes and all types of hygiene products available for use and they are free to take items home.  I have a "lending closet" where patients can check out books, learning games, sensory development items and more.  I have my exam room divided into two halves, separated by an accordion wall and the "interview" side has a loveseat for the patients to sit on and there is local art and flowers to look at and they don't have to focus on all the medical equipment.  I have a "spinning chair" that kids (or adults) can use at any time.  I also sit in a comfortable overstuffed chair so that the patient's understand I am not in a hurry, I am here to listen to them and that I do honestly want to get to know them. I have a clock strategically positioned so I can glance at it without making a patient feel rushed.  I have my entire office/exam area set up intentionally with complex trauma in mind.  I don't sit between patients and the door, the couch is against a wall so no one can sneak up on them, patients can see all the doors when they walk in a room, I have white noise to help with sound hypervigilance.  Unless a patient is in the patient bathroom, I keep the door open so patients can reassure themselves no one is in there. Initially I hated having a laptop between me and the patient, but as time went on, especially after covid started, I found sending prescriptions/orders/referrals while sitting in the patient room not only was more efficient, but patients feel empowered to advocate for themselves with labs and pharmacies when they claim they hadn't received the orders (a very common and serious problem in my rural area). One of the most important things I find my patients value is a very simple (non)policy.  I do not have a "missed appointment" or "no show" policy.  If a patient no shows or doesn't call or misses an appointment or cancels after the fact, it is not a problem.  I go out of my way to never make them feel guilty or judged. 
 There is no charge and I will not "fire" a patient for missing appointments. And appointments can be converted to telemedicine even if they were scheduled in person.  For many of my patients with mental health issues, telemedicine has changed their lives, allowing them to have appointments even when their symptoms are too severe to leave their homes.  This very simple policy which really is not of any consequence to me, has increased trust and improved patient relationships in numerous ways.
ypTreatment4: I received a CT report on one of my patients from an ED visit that revealed an intraabdominal mass with likely metastases to lung, liver, lymph nodes and bone.  Knowing my patient had poor health literacy and would not have asked the ED physician many questions, I called her and asked her to come in for a visit.  I met with her, her adult children and her granddaughter who is a nurse after my usual clinic hours so we would not be interrupted.  We spent nearly an hour discussing goals of care, her fears and what she wanted as far as interventions.  At the end of the visit, I made a referral to hospice and signed the patients DNR paperwork.  The patient and her family thanked me for my time and hugged me.  Even when I was giving very bad news, I was able to do it in a way that the patient felt heard and understood.  I also reached out to the patient when I got the report, rather than wait for them to contact me, which she greatly appreciated. I still find it hard when patients thank me after I give them bad news, but from their point of view they appreciate the compassion and honesty I use when approaching difficult conversations.

sayingTreatment:
Congratulations on reaching this pivotal moment in your career! Starting your journey as a healthcare provider is both exciting and daunting. You’ve spent years preparing for this, and now, you’ll finally put your knowledge into practice. While your medical education has equipped you with the skills to diagnose and treat, there’s an essential aspect of healthcare that goes beyond clinical knowledge—the art of truly connecting with your patients and meeting them where they are.

When I first started, I was eager to demonstrate everything I’d learned. But soon, I realized that the most effective care comes from understanding not just the illness but the person behind it. Patients come from all walks of life, with diverse backgrounds, beliefs, and expectations. It's easy to get caught up in the clinical side of things, but the heart of healthcare is empathy and connection.

I remember one patient vividly—a middle-aged man who had been diagnosed with diabetes. He had missed several appointments and wasn’t following his treatment plan. It would have been easy to label him as “non-compliant” and move on. But instead, I took the time to listen. I learned that he worked two jobs, had limited access to healthy food, and was overwhelmed by the complexities of managing his condition. By understanding his perspective, we were able to tailor a treatment plan that fit his life. We focused on small, achievable goals, and I connected him with resources that made healthy choices more accessible. Over time, he became more engaged in his care, and his health began to improve.

ypTreatment1_2: If they feel like you "understand them" or understand their stiuation and truly care for them, they are more likely to be compliant with the treatment plan. manipCheckOpen_T: Physicians better understanding patients & patient-centered care to provide better care and outcomes for patients.
sayingTreatment: It is important to get to know your patient and try to best understand their situation so as to maximize their care and best position them for a positive outcome.  It is important to try your best to fully explain their diagnosis and all treatment options (risks, benefits, etc) at their level, and then come up with the treatment plan that they are most comfortable with and not be paternalistic in your approach.  For instance, I often give patients/family the option to empirically treat an injury based on their history, physical exam, x-ray findings (or lack thereof), and my experience and then get an MRI later if they don't get better, versus getting an MRI right away (if insurance authorizes) and then coming up with a treatment plan after the MRI.  I want to do what makes the patient or parents most comfortable and gives them the most re-assurance, including taking finances into consideration - if they can't afford or don't want to pay the MRI co-pay/deductable, then that is fine as long as I feel it is safe to hold off on getting an MRI.  On the other hand, other patients want more information right away, which is also fine, even though I would be comfortable treating first without getting an MRI or that is not how I would approach it if I was the patient.

sayingTreatment: Remember, what made you want to be a physician?  If you don’t, then, at least remind yourself that every patient is someone’s parent, family member, friend, special someone in someone’s life. If you remember that, and treat every patient with respect and think of them as someone who deserves the best care there is, I believe you will, also see the beauty and privilege of being a physician caring for patients in this underserved community/FQHC. From the humility, you see in these patients, you will soon realize that they will remind you of your aunt or your uncle, cousin, niece, or someone special in your life, that you want to make sure that they live a very healthy life. You will also realize that not all of them will understand everything that you say and that you have to repeated multiple times and remind them of what they have to take and what they shouldn’t take (like bringing up your sharpie and marking the bottle with numbers and symbols as well as big black X for things that you do not want them to take anymore bc your patients just can’t read.) if you speak humbly to your patients, and you find out why it is that they aren’t doing something, they will absolutely open up to you and let you know what their barriers to a healthy life is, and why they are and aren’t taking certain medication. Not everyone is booksmart like us so we do need to be cognizant of how we speak to our patients as well. I always believed in treating others the way we want to be treated, and so with that in mind, being sensitive to our patients’ shame, fear, anxiety, or any other emotion you can see on their face or their voice, will truly guide you in the right direction as you continue to practice the most difficult of jobs — being a primary care physician — having to answer to every question that a patient has about their health and not health, as well as the health of their family members, and being bombarded with all the quality metrics that you must make sure is covered, while addressing their 15 problems that they want you to help them with.
ypTreatment3_1: First of all, I always try to show my patients that I respect them as a person, and that there are free and welcome to choose any physician they want, but if they keep coming to me that we have to work together to improve their health so that they can achieve whatever goals they have in life, whether it is to spend time with their family members, work until past retirement age, go spend six months in their home country after retirement, etc. So with this in mind, I always make sure to know how they get to clinic. Whether they drive independently, and because I work in FQHC I have a lot of patience, taking public transportation like the bus. So I’ve never said no to patients who are late and they know that , I understand their circumstances and I won’t get mad if they’re late and I will still see them. Furthermore, I always spend more time past minutes that I usually get in one patient visit and I often fall behind. But every time I’m with the patient I give them 110% of my attention and they know that because they’re able to ask all the questions and I answer every single one of them.  And I will never rush them either. Because of that, my patience and die have develop a very good high-quality patient patient doctor relationship. Furthermore I also always have in my ER. Their medical insurance type listed because I used to have a lot of insured patients as well as Medi-Cal patients and with that in mind, I tend to , think about how they will pay for certain services or what it’s covered and what isn’t. And if it’s something that’s not covered then what can I do to provide them a low cost alternative. My patient all really appreciate me for thinking of that. Other examples like making a telephone visit for follow up so they don’t have to pay for the in person, co-pay, and other strategies like that where I think about what it would cost them has always made my patients feel like i have the best in mind for them.
ypTreatment4: I had a middle-age woman that I already knew had extreme anxiety when it comes to needles and she had been diagnosed with diabetes about five years ago and was in denial for a while and wasn’t taking her medication. I didn’t know that she would never want to start insulin and so it had taken me a while to get her up to five oral medication‘s. I wish time her A1c was still not well controlled. so I worked with her to figure out if there was someone in her household like her partner and spouse who could actually do a weekly injection instead to help her better regulate her sugars and be more likely to adhere to the regimen. Knowing that she would not be able to inject herself, I wanted to bring in people who care for her and would be able to make her take her medication if they helped her. With this in mind, her husband was able to come into the visit with her and have me explain to him and her together then importance of medication adherence, and due time her anxiety related to needles went down because she realized that she wouldn’t have to be the one injecting herself. Overtime, her diabetes also improved. So I do find that being able to meet the patients were specially anxious, where they at, and find an alternative so that they can feel less anxious , it’s always the better approach to being realistic in terms of medication adherence

sayingTreatment: Remember, what made you want to be a physician?  If you don’t, then, at least remind yourself that every patient is someone’s parent, family member, friend, special someone in someone’s life. If you remember that, and treat every patient with respect and think of them as someone who deserves the best care there is, I believe you will, also see the beauty and privilege of being a physician caring for patients in this underserved community/FQHC. From the humility, you see in these patients, you will soon realize that they will remind you of your aunt or your uncle, cousin, niece, or someone special in your life, that you want to make sure that they live a very healthy life. You will also realize that not all of them will understand everything that you say and that you have to repeated multiple times and remind them of what they have to take and what they shouldn’t take (like bringing up your sharpie and marking the bottle with numbers and symbols as well as big black X for things that you do not want them to take anymore bc your patients just can’t read.) if you speak humbly to your patients, and you find out why it is that they aren’t doing something, they will absolutely open up to you and let you know what their barriers to a healthy life is, and why they are and aren’t taking certain medication. Not everyone is booksmart like us so we do need to be cognizant of how we speak to our patients as well. I always believed in treating others the way we want to be treated, and so with that in mind, being sensitive to our patients’ shame, fear, anxiety, or any other emotion you can see on their face or their voice, will truly guide you in the right direction as you continue to practice the most difficult of jobs — being a primary care physician — having to answer to every question that a patient has about their health and not health, as well as the health of their family members, and being bombarded with all the quality metrics that you must make sure is covered, while addressing their 15 problems that they want you to help them with.
ypTreatment3_1: First of all, I always try to show my patients that I respect them as a person, and that there are free and welcome to choose any physician they want, but if they keep coming to me that we have to work together to improve their health so that they can achieve whatever goals they have in life, whether it is to spend time with their family members, work until past retirement age, go spend six months in their home country after retirement, etc. So with this in mind, I always make sure to know how they get to clinic. Whether they drive independently, and because I work in FQHC I have a lot of patience, taking public transportation like the bus. So I’ve never said no to patients who are late and they know that , I understand their circumstances and I won’t get mad if they’re late and I will still see them. Furthermore, I always spend more time past minutes that I usually get in one patient visit and I often fall behind. But every time I’m with the patient I give them 110% of my attention and they know that because they’re able to ask all the questions and I answer every single one of them.  And I will never rush them either. Because of that, my patience and die have develop a very good high-quality patient patient doctor relationship. Furthermore I also always have in my ER. Their medical insurance type listed because I used to have a lot of insured patients as well as Medi-Cal patients and with that in mind, I tend to , think about how they will pay for certain services or what it’s covered and what isn’t. And if it’s something that’s not covered then what can I do to provide them a low cost alternative. My patient all really appreciate me for thinking of that. Other examples like making a telephone visit for follow up so they don’t have to pay for the in person, co-pay, and other strategies like that where I think about what it would cost them has always made my patients feel like i have the best in mind for them.
ypTreatment4: I had a middle-age woman that I already knew had extreme anxiety when it comes to needles and she had been diagnosed with diabetes about five years ago and was in denial for a while and wasn’t taking her medication. I didn’t know that she would never want to start insulin and so it had taken me a while to get her up to five oral medication‘s. I wish time her A1c was still not well controlled. so I worked with her to figure out if there was someone in her household like her partner and spouse who could actually do a weekly injection instead to help her better regulate her sugars and be more likely to adhere to the regimen. Knowing that she would not be able to inject herself, I wanted to bring in people who care for her and would be able to make her take her medication if they helped her. sayingTreatment: Medicine is exciting.  Learning about the body and treatments is great.  You will be seen as a leader of your community.  People will talk about you, because you hold a title.  That is exciting at first...then it can feel like a burden at times. Ask any doctor who has been in practice for a decade and often they say the thing that keeps them happy and going is getting to know their patients.  However, in hospital settings (with many primary care docs in the employment model) there are pressures to see a certain number of patients.  Please be strong, you can have some control over your schedule, even if it seems like you do not.  Ask your staff to schedule 30 minute appointments for the patients who often want to talk.  It will keep you closer to being on schedule and you will not dread the patient who comes in wanting to talk, but rather, you'll enjoy the conversations.  It may mean less billing and may upset some administrator who only thinks of money, but push on!  Balance your schedule well.  Have fun.  Remember what a joy it is that we get to do this and be a part of very intimate aspects of patients' lives. They will pray for you.  You may have 2500 patients, but they have one doctor.

valuesOpenTreatment_3: I think taking a holistic approach is one of my biggest values. I was trained to regard the patient as a whole, taking into account their physical, mental, and spiritual health when treating them. Many medical problems people come in with are multifaceted, and other parts of their lives besides their physical health need to be addressed.
manipCheckOpen_T: Today I read about different ways to improve the doctor-patient relationship, and how having a strong relationship leads to better outcomes for patients.
sayingTreatment:
Welcome to the world of direct patient care. It is scary and overwhelming, but with time becomes fulfilling and manageable. It is very easy to lose sight of what your job is when you get bogged down in the daily tasks that need to be done. It is important to take a step back and remember that you are taking care of a human, and to see patients as people and not units of work. Often the most rewarding part of healthcare is connecting with a patient and watching your interventions make a difference in their life. 

One thing that has helped me tremendously has been to learn about not just the medical parts of a patient, but also their social history. Where they live, what they do, their familial and personal relationships, and their goals in life play a huge role in how they view healthcare. Anticipating and identifying barriers to treatment will go a long way towards taking better care of your patients.
ypTreatment3_1: One way I try to connect with patients is to ask them where they are from and about their hometown. I also ask about family they have or hobbies they take part in. Then when I see them on subsequent visits, I’ll bring up what we discussed last time to show that I remember them as a person and have invested in them and their health. I also try to be as honest with patients as possible, and tell them candidly what I’m thinking and what their medical problems are. If I don’t know something, I will admit it to them, but also say that I will look into it for them. I feel that being open and honest lets them see my human side as well, which helps foster a relationship between us.
ypTreatment4: There was a patient I had with metastatic lung cancer who was very fearful about getting treatment. I had been taking care of him for a while and over time we built a trusting relationship by bonding over his family. One day he was particularly anxious about going to get simulated for brain radiation. We had a prolonged talk about why he was anxious and what his goals were in life. I often referenced back to his family that we had talked about earlier to let him know that I was on his side and wants the best for him. Eventually he was able to calm down and went for the treatment. I feel that had I not had this background relationship with the patient prior to this episode, he would not have agreed to get the radiation treatment.

I was trained to regard the patient as a whole, taking into account their physical, mental, and spiritual health when treating them. sayingTreatment:
Welcome to the world of direct patient care. It is scary and overwhelming, but with time becomes fulfilling and manageable. It is very easy to lose sight of what your job is when you get bogged down in the daily tasks that need to be done. It is important to take a step back and remember that you are taking care of a human, and to see patients as people and not units of work. Often the most rewarding part of healthcare is connecting with a patient and watching your interventions make a difference in their life. 

One thing that has helped me tremendously has been to learn about not just the medical parts of a patient, but also their social history. Where they live, what they do, their familial and personal relationships, and their goals in life play a huge role in how they view healthcare. Anticipating and identifying barriers to treatment will go a long way towards taking better care of your patients.
ypTreatment3_1: One way I try to connect with patients is to ask them where they are from and about their hometown. I also ask about family they have or hobbies they take part in. Then when I see them on subsequent visits, I’ll bring up what we discussed last time to show that I remember them as a person and have invested in them and their health. I also try to be as honest with patients as possible, and tell them candidly what I’m thinking and what their medical problems are. If I don’t know something, I will admit it to them, but also say that I will look into it for them. I feel that being open and honest lets them see my human side as well, which helps foster a relationship between us.
ypTreatment4: There was a patient I had with metastatic lung cancer who was very fearful about getting treatment. I had been taking care of him for a while and over time we built a trusting relationship by bonding over his family. One day he was particularly anxious about going to get simulated for brain radiation. We had a prolonged talk about why he was anxious and what his goals were in life. I often referenced back to his family that we had talked about earlier to let him know that I was on his side and wants the best for him. Eventually he was able to calm down and went for the treatment. I feel that had I not had this background relationship with the patient prior to this episode, he would not have agreed to get the radiation treatment.

sayingTreatment:
Welcome to practice of Medicine.  Our profession is not as glamorous as they portray it on the TV screen.  A lot of personal and family sacrifices have to be made. There will be many last minute cancellations of family activities due to emergency calls. It is a high stress profession as people’s lives depend on you. Your medical decisions will be life changing for a lot of the patients so we have to be very judicious when we advise our patients and make medical recommendations. However, we also have the opportunity to help them feel better about themselves, to help them get healthier and able to spend more time with their friends and loved ones.  Some patients may be confrontational when they come to see you, but it would be prudent to bear in mind that they may already be having a very bad day at home and they are worried about their medical issues. Show compassion, patience, and honesty when taking care of the patients. Remember that one day, we will be a patient too, and we would want our doctor to exhibit these qualities. 

Foods for thought:
1. Treat others the way you would like to be treated.
2. Respect is not demanded.  It is earned. 
3. When treating patients with complicated issues, remember that it is more fortuitous to be on the treating (giving) side than the receiving end. 

LET US GO AND SAVE SOME LIVES!!!

We’re all influenced by the culture and Society and specific neighborhood in which we were raised and we come to the patient encounters with different ideas about our overall health And the things that impact that. Patient bring to the table A lifetime of learned behaviors, and internalized beliefs about medicine, health, and the healthcare system - If you don’t meet them where they are, you’ll never make progress together as a patient and a healthcare provider.

sayingTreatment:
A common phrase among healthcare workers is, “healthcare is a team sport.” This is definitely true regarding interdisciplinary care, but I also think perhaps the most important “team” forms between the provider and the patient (and their families).
Taking the extra time to get to know your patients outside of their diagnosis, identify their hesitations and baseline understandings, and form longitudinal relationships (whether this is just over the course of their hospital stay, or over several years of seeing the patient in the clinic) increases patient buy-in and sense of agency over their health. 
Always remember, you may see 20 patients in a day, but each of those patients is (usually) only seen one doctor. The handful of minutes you spend with each one can change the trajectory of not only their day, but also their life.
ypTreatment3_1:
I tried to learn a little bit about every single patient’s non-medical history, such as what they do or did for a living, what they enjoy to do in their free time, Their children or spouses names, Etc. I tried to make note of these in a secure location within the EMR and refresh myself on these details prior to my next appointment with the patient. Typically a very personal connection, and helps patient to realize that I really do care about them as people rather than just another office visit or prescription to write.
Additionally, I try to explain in non-medical terms what their medication’s do and what they are treating. I like to explain the medical reasoning behind certain prescriptions, if applicable — for example, for a patient with a new diagnosis of heart failure I always included discussion of important medication’s that we will be initiating over the next several office visits and I highlight/emphasize the reason behind the specific medication’s that data actually shows they will prolong this patient’s life and improve their quality of life. That helps patients have more buy-in for medically necessary therapies as well as helps them understand that I’m not writing prescriptions just to satisfy “Big Pharma” but because they have a real and measurable impact on the patient’s life.
ypTreatment4: I work in a practice with several Other physicians, which means it’s not uncommon for patients to be seen by multiple Providers over the course of several visits. I always make a point to have my patience who are more hesitant or anxious to only be scheduled with me rather than a different physician. I found that this continuity of care increases their trust and comfort with the healthcare system, as well as with our practice. Months ago, I happen to notice a scheduling anomaly in which several of my patients were mistakenly scheduled with a variety of other physicians, so I had my nurse reach out to the patient directly to reschedule with me. One of these patients had her follow up appointment Recently and she made a point to directly thank me for reaching out to reschedule so that she could see me personally. Normal relationships absolutely encourage patient buy-in, and when they realize that you made a point to be the one to follow up with them, they have more trust in your motives and your desire to do right by them

valuesOpenTreatment_3: Being able to empathize with my patience affords me better insight into their problems and concerns and their perceived understanding of the situation. It also helps foster my patients’ trust in the care I’m providing for them.
manipCheckOpen_T: I read about the importance of establishing patients’ trust in their providers to promote improved care and quality of life.
sayingTreatment: Having worked several jobs and various fields prior to matriculating into medical school, I can attest that no job is as rewarding or as mentally taxing as being a healthcare provider. You’ll have days that lift you up and inspire you to do all you can for each and every patient. You’ll have other days to get you down, the ones where you lose a patient or patients. No matter what kind of day you have, always do your best and what’s right for every patient. Strive to always empathize and try to understand each patient as the individual person that they are. Each patient presents with their own unique problems, concerns, fears, and goals. Make sure that you are doing your best as a physician and as a person to give them the utmost in care. Understanding your patients and having them establish their trust in you is key to ensuring that their care and quality of life are maximized.
ypTreatment3_1: I try to spend additional time getting to know patients and where they come from on a personal level, especially during their first appointment with me. I’ll spend a few minutes at the beginning of each visit catching up with what’s been going on in their lives since I last saw them. I also try to tease out their individual socioeconomic status to customize treatment plans that are reasonable in regard to cost, frequency, and complexity for each patient.
ypTreatment4: I had an extremely pleasant patient with metastatic disease that was well known to our medical center, including myself, that was admitted again close to the end of his life for similar complaints as previous admissions (SOB, chest pain, decreased appetite). This time, his demeanor was markedly different. He was loud, combative, and refused to discuss any meaningful care plans with the overnight provider who admitted him. The overnight provider wasn’t familiar with the patient and believed that he was simply a difficult patient at baseline. Immediately upon seeing him at bedside, I realized that he had now become anxious and fearful about the end of his life rapidly approaching. I got on one knee at his bedside and held his hand (I absolutely believe in the power of touch) while reminding him of who I was and how well I knew his situation. In doing so, I was able to bring his anxiety level down enough for us to have a meaningful conversation regarding his new fears and realizations regarding his condition.

valuesOpenTreatment_3: knowledge. I'd like to start with the google search for everything. Knowing what they have read and following up with guidelines and protocols helps build a patient's trust. However, there are time when it can be tricky because sometimes when you say something that they don't like or the damn internet says otherwise, you have to play the game and reiterate what the updated guidelines are. All in and you speak with conviction because if not, you are fu*ked.
ypTreatment1_1: Let's go to culture. Some cultures disapprove of the 'American' way. They explain that "well it's done in Europe" so why can't I do that here? Holy moly! This has to be followed with what exactly do you know about that? Where the pt. feels as if they are being challenged. That gets tricky. After explaining why things are done here the way they are, there is still disapproval. As a result, I have to basically give up my explanations. Here is where I say, you can do what you feel is best, however, please realize (medical terms, medical explanation, human explanation) is in the best interest for you.  Listening and nodding to their perspectives at least helps the pt. feel heard. While time is an issue where I work, I try to keep them at ease by listening. Once they are done, I tell the pt I have heard their perspective, I respect their perspective and then mention, that I hope they take my suggesting as part of their perspective. Some will agree, some will not and documentation of such is vital!
ypTreatment1_2: They want to know that they still have the final say. This helps their confidence. I am not an omnipotent being and I want the pt. to keep holding the wheel so to speak.
ypTreatment2_1: Well, nowadays it's hard to get an appointment right away for many patients. Right there, when someone is worried and the office says oh the Doctor/PA/NP is not available until X month...this leads to being anxious. Patients hesitate to ask questions if you are speaking fast and speaking like you know it all. Fact is we as HC professionals do not know it all. Another reason for anxiety or hesitation to ask questions is because they don't understand what is being said to them, they are elderly and/or the medical jargon may as well be a foreign language. Pt's also get anxious or hesitate to ask questions when you have given a determinant treatment, they will get all better so why ask questions? This is a long conversation O, I hope that what I wrote makes sense.
ypTreatment2_1.1: 38Y F with HIV, G1P0, works as a correction officer, PMHx +HIV, low viral load on HIIV antivirals. Pregnant @9M, partner did not know she was HIV+. Centered the pt: discussed risks of holding this information from her partner. Got to know pt. personally: Able to discuss how she acquired HIV, what her job was like and how hard it was for her to have relationships.  She opened up about past relationships, intimacy with them and when she opened up about HIV, everyone leaves right away. She didn't want her current partner to leave her. Built trust: Explained that our team would support her to explain to her partner her current status. Tried to make sure she felt comfortable and would not worry about being left alone or had lack of support when she would build up the courage to tell her partner that she was HIV+. BRUTAL
manipCheckOpen_T: Patient perspective, Patient trust
sayingTreatment:
It's been a long road. There will be happy times when you know what you have done is for a patient's greater good because VOILA!, they are cured! The reality is that there will be troubles that you only read in the news and things just so bizarre. Stay cool. Fret not, take a deep breathe and learn how to listen without saying I'm sorry. Sorry is what you say when you want permission to stop feeling bad. A pt. doesn't want to hear you say sorry, a lot of them want you to say what can be done, how he/she can gear up for the battle that awaits. And while the gear is good, there are times when that gear needs changes and each battle is a different story. Each battle doesn't lessen their fear, their anxiety so It's up to you to help them play it out at all defensive/offensive positions. So get ready, know how to play. 
All you have to do is listen and make sure your patient is heard. If you get that down, that's half the battle. 
One more thing, know to take of yourself. Love yourself and know when you can't do this. Take the time out to stare out of the window and look out at the sky. It is a beautiful world after all. Appreciate yourself and what you do. As a side note, Thank you for all you do, for those pt's that might not say thank you. Because those exist as well. Last, You are here for a reason and the rewards of a smile, of trust from someone you didn't know 5 minutes ago, is priceless. 
All the best to you.

valuesOpenTreatment_3: knowledge. I'd like to start with the google search for everything. Knowing what they have read and following up with guidelines and protocols helps build a patient's trust. However, there are time when it can be tricky because sometimes when you say something that they don't like or the damn internet says otherwise, you have to play the game and reiterate what the updated guidelines are. All in and you speak with conviction because if not, you are fu*ked.
ypTreatment1_1: Let's go to culture. Some cultures disapprove of the 'American' way. They explain that "well it's done in Europe" so why can't I do that here? Holy moly! This has to be followed with what exactly do you know about that? Where the pt. feels as if they are being challenged. That gets tricky. After explaining why things are done here the way they are, there is still disapproval. As a result, I have to basically give up my explanations. Here is where I say, you can do what you feel is best, however, please realize (medical terms, medical explanation, human explanation) is in the best interest for you.  Listening and nodding to their perspectives at least helps the pt. feel heard. While time is an issue where I work, I try to keep them at ease by listening. Once they are done, I tell the pt I have heard their perspective, I respect their perspective and then mention, that I hope they take my suggesting as part of their perspective. Some will agree, some will not and documentation of such is vital!
ypTreatment1_2: They want to know that they still have the final say. This helps their confidence. I am not an omnipotent being and I want the pt. to keep holding the wheel so to speak.
ypTreatment2_1: Well, nowadays it's hard to get an appointment right away for many patients. Right there, when someone is worried and the office says oh the Doctor/PA/NP is not available until X month...this leads to being anxious. Patients hesitate to ask questions if you are speaking fast and speaking like you know it all. Fact is we as HC professionals do not know it all. Another reason for anxiety or hesitation to ask questions is because they don't understand what is being said to them, they are elderly and/or the medical jargon may as well be a foreign language. Pt's also get anxious or hesitate to ask questions when you have given a determinant treatment, they will get all better so why ask questions? This is a long conversation O, I hope that what I wrote makes sense.
ypTreatment2_1.1: 38Y F with HIV, G1P0, works as a correction officer, PMHx +HIV, low viral load on HIIV antivirals. Pregnant @9M, partner did not know she was HIV+. Centered the pt: discussed risks of holding this information from her partner. Got to know pt. personally: Able to discuss how she acquired HIV, what her job was like and how hard it was for her to have relationships.  She opened up about past relationships, intimacy with them and when she opened up about HIV, everyone leaves right away. She didn't want her current partner to leave her. Built trust: Explained that our team would support her to explain to her partner her current status. Tried to make sure she felt comfortable and would not worry about being left alone or had lack of support when she would build up the courage to tell her partner that she was HIV+. BRUTAL

sayingTreatment:
It's been a long road. There will be happy times when you know what you have done is for a patient's greater good because VOILA!, they are cured! The reality is that there will be troubles that you only read in the news and things just so bizarre. Stay cool. Fret not, take a deep breathe and learn how to listen without saying I'm sorry. Sorry is what you say when you want permission to stop feeling bad. A pt. doesn't want to hear you say sorry, a lot of them want you to say what can be done, how he/she can gear up for the battle that awaits. And while the gear is good, there are times when that gear needs changes and each battle is a different story. Each battle doesn't lessen their fear, their anxiety so It's up to you to help them play it out at all defensive/offensive positions. So get ready, know how to play. 
All you have to do is listen and make sure your patient is heard. If you get that down, that's half the battle. 
One more thing, know to take of yourself. Love yourself and know when you can't do this. Take the time out to stare out of the window and look out at the sky. It is a beautiful world after all. Appreciate yourself and what you do. As a side note, Thank you for all you do, for those pt's that might not say thank you. Because those exist as well. Last, You are here for a reason and the rewards of a smile, of trust from someone you didn't know 5 minutes ago, is priceless. 
All the best to you.

valuesOpenTreatment_3: Empathy is the most important attribute.  I place myself in the patients situation to understand how my actions and approaches best relate to them.  I try to view their situation from my own personal standpoint
ypTreatment1_1: It is critical to understand patients' perspectives and why they take certain actions because we want them to comply with the treatments and diagnostic protocols.  If we don't understand the patients, we are making assumptions based on our own culture and morals that might not align with the patients' perspectives.  Then compliance will suffer due to a lack of understanding and appreciation on our part

Use and appreciate the patient's body language and posture.  Be aware of your body language and posture. Ask them to explain their comments about their home life or social situation.

valuesOpenTreatment_3: My perception is that patients do not always feed that they are heard.   Being empathetic and showing that their thoughts and feelings are valued, shared helps to validate them and garner a level of trust.  From a treatment perspective, a holostic approach also helps navigate patients individual needs and situation.  It also helps to frame the patients need and values that are unique to them and offers opportunities for shared decision making.  Mecidibr should always be used to make our society a better place.
manipCheckOpen_T: We read about what healthcare providers value in their strategies in proving care to patients and how these can be employed to achieve alignment and optimal outcomes though enhanced doctor patient relationships.
sayingTreatment:
As you navigate the busy field of healthcare, always keep these tenants in mind:
Never pass up an opportunity for patients to direct their care when several options of equal outcome exist.  As these decisions affect them the most, allowing for shared decision making is a powerful way to build trust.
Allowing patients and families to define their priorities will provide insight as to how to structure their treatment plan, gain trust, and remove barriers.
Proving medical knowledge and insights good, but also support, reassurance, and proving a safe forum for patients to be heard and feelings validated brings a humanistic element that is required for success in medicine, and devoid in much of today’s culture.

It is privilege to have the trust, insight, and impacts on so many people’s lives…. Use it wisely.
ypTreatment3_1: We employ multiple strategies such as direct questioning about their goals, prioritizies, and desires for care.  If we do not have the same goal in mind, the treatment plan will never succeed.  Secondly, allowing choices when possible.  How can we achieve this success together.  If we can co design the treatment plan, than more adherence/ buy in can be achieved.  Lastly,  questioning where they feel they have the biggest barriers and will need extra support so that we can proactively design strategies to manage and support these.
ypTreatment4: We had a patient that needed surgery and was very reluctant to proceed.  She had seen multiple providers over the past several years who made the same recommendation.  After providing her with recommendations for care though, we had an in-depth conversation as why she had followed though with previous recommendations for care.  Ultimately, we took the time to address her fears, validate them, and then design a strategy on how we could successfully overcome them to meet her longer term goal of improving her health and activity level.  I think the opportunity to vocalize and address these fears in a supportive manner was instrumental In gaining her trust which ultimately led to her pursuing the more invasive treatment option that she had been hesitant in the past.

ypTreatment1_2: Understanding a patient's perspective can significantly enhance his/her recovery. ypTreatment2_1.1: I remember one of my patients was a retired engineer with a history of chronic fatigue. By addressing these underlying factors, I was able to provide a more comprehensive treatment plan that included not only medical interventions but also lifestyle changes and counseling. sayingTreatment:
As you embark on your journey in the medical field, remember that the most effective care is often centered around the patient. By understanding and aligning with your patients' goals, you can foster a sense of self-efficacy and empower them to take ownership of their health. Small changes in your approach, such as adopting a patient-centered approach during visits, can significantly improve trust and build strong patient-physician relationships.

       Moreover, demonstrating sensitivity to the challenges your patients may face can make a world of difference. By acknowledging their circumstances and providing support, you can encourage active participation in their healthcare and improve compliance with treatment plans. Remember, your role extends beyond diagnosis and treatment; it's about empowering patients to lead healthier lives.

sayingTreatment: Congratulations on choosing a career in medicine! The journey ahead may be long and difficult, but the knowledge you will gain during your journey can be used to improve the lives of your fellow human beings. Remember, you are not  your patients father. You are not your patients boss. You are not your patients commanding officer. You can not make your patients take medications, undergo testing, or endure procedures. You are simply an advisor. Instead of dictating to your patients, let your patients know that you are advising them, with the goal of improving their health and well-being. You will encounter patients that are frustrating and difficult to deal with. Rather than getting upset, try to understand why your patients feel the way they do, and meet them where they are.

A US Marine for example may not complain of pain until it is a severe medical emergency when it would have been better to report pain earlier. ypTreatment1_2: It enables one to better understand the disease process to generate a more accurate diagnosis and tailor treatment such as pain control for optimal management
ypTreatment2_1: Firstly there is a power differential inherent with the patient-provider interaction. Combine this with issues such as language barriers, health literacy barriers and anxiety from being sick and it becomes self-evident why patients may hesitate to ask questions. Additionally, certain vulnerable populations have historically been violated or ignored by the medical establishment which also would make someone hesitate to ask questions
ypTreatment2_1.1: I had a female patient with chronic abdominal issues come in to see me for the first time. She had been previously informed she only had gas or this was due to her menstrual issues. I saw her for the first time and asked her to tell me what issues the abdominal pain was impacting, what bodily functions she was having trouble with. Upon this she told me she had been having urinary incontinence as something seems to be poking out "down there". I performed an examination and found a significant bladder prolapse but also a palpable abdominal mass that upon imaging was 6cm large. Luckily it ended being a benign leiomyoma that had caused such intraabdominal pressure that she ended up having bladder prolapse but it could have easily been a leiomyosarcoma or ovarian tumor, etc
manipCheckOpen_T: How patients can find it difficult to trust/ask questions
sayingTreatment: I want to congratulate you on the exciting road ahead but I want you to know that you have the lives of people in your hands whom are turning to you at their most vulnerable. Please be mindful of the trust they place in your hands and include not just their symptoms but also the context within which these symptoms exist when taking care of them. Be aware that their cultural or socioeconomic backgrounds can impact their disease process and so encourage them to open up to you so you can understand how they are being impacted within the context in which they live. This will help them trust you more helping not only their present recovery but improving their quality of life throughout their time with you. Build goals with them within their context so that they feel empowered to take ownership of their health, an evidence-based approach to ensure patients' mental and physical well-being and recovery. However, try to steer away from stereotyping them and don't ignore their pain for this will be to your detriment. Instead try to get to the root cause of their pain whether it be physical or psychological or both.

valuesOpenTreatment_3: I prioritize sensitivity by recognizing and respecting the diverse backgrounds of my patients. Through empathy, I strive to take my patients’ perspectives, allowing me to identify and understand their emotions and experiences. I am committed to enhancing my knowledge of practical interpersonal skills to build trust with my patients. Additionally, I am dedicated to continuous learning to deepen my understanding of my patients and their unique circumstances.   This approach is important because it fosters a compassionate and trusting environment, improves patient communication, and ensures that care is tailored to each individual's needs, ultimately leading to better patient outcomes.
ypTreatment1_1: Understanding patients' perspectives and their reasons for their actions is critical because it allows healthcare providers to offer more personalized and effective care. By seeing the world through the patients' eyes, providers can identify underlying factors that influence their behavior, such as cultural beliefs, personal values, or past experiences. This understanding fosters trust, improves communication, and enhances patient compliance with treatment plans. It also helps in addressing any fears or misconceptions patients may have, leading to more empathetic and respectful care that meets their unique needs and circumstances. Ultimately, it contributes to better health outcomes and a more positive patient experience.
ypTreatment1_2:
Understanding a patient's perspective can have a significant positive influence on both the patient and their recovery. When healthcare providers take the time to truly understand a patient’s feelings, beliefs, and motivations, it helps in building a strong therapeutic relationship based on trust and mutual respect. This connection can make patients feel heard, valued, and supported, reducing anxiety and increasing their willingness to engage in their treatment plan.

Additionally, understanding their perspective allows providers to tailor interventions that align with the patient’s values and lifestyle, making it more likely for them to adhere to the recommended treatments. It also enables healthcare providers to address any barriers or concerns the patient may have, such as fear of side effects or cultural hesitations, thus improving compliance. Overall, this approach not only enhances the patient’s emotional well-being but also promotes active participation in their own care, leading to improved recovery rates and better overall health outcomes.
ypTreatment2_1:
Patients may feel anxious or hesitant to ask questions for several reasons. Commonly, they might fear that their questions will seem silly or that they’ll be judged for not understanding medical jargon or complex information. Some patients worry about taking up too much of the healthcare provider’s time, especially if they perceive that the provider is busy or rushed. There can also be a power dynamic at play, where patients feel intimidated or uncomfortable challenging the authority of a healthcare professional.

Cultural factors may also contribute; in some cultures, questioning a doctor is considered disrespectful. Additionally, past negative experiences with healthcare providers, where patients felt dismissed or not listened to, can make them reluctant to speak up. Finally, anxiety or embarrassment about their health condition can make patients feel vulnerable, leading them to hold back on asking questions they genuinely want answers to. Understanding these reasons is crucial for healthcare providers to create a more open, supportive environment that encourages patient engagement and communication.
ypTreatment2_1.1:
I recall working with a patient who was visibly anxious and hesitant to engage during her appointments. She was dealing with a chronic condition that required lifestyle changes, but she was struggling to follow through with the recommendations. Instead of focusing solely on the medical aspects of her care, I took a step back and made an effort to center her as a person, not just a patient. I began by asking open-ended questions about her life—her family, work, and what she enjoyed doing in her free time. 

Through these conversations, I learned that she was overwhelmed with her responsibilities at home, which made it difficult for her to prioritize her health. She shared stories about her children and her worries about being a burden to them. By listening without judgment and acknowledging her concerns, I was able to show her that I genuinely cared about her as an individual. This approach helped build trust, and over time, she became more comfortable sharing her fears and asking questions about her care. 

We worked together to develop a plan that accommodated her lifestyle, focusing on small, manageable steps rather than overwhelming changes. By centering the patient, getting to know her personally, and building trust, she felt more supported and empowered, which significantly improved her adherence to the treatment plan and ultimately her health outcomes. This experience reinforced the importance of truly seeing and hearing the patient beyond their medical condition.

sayingTreatment:
Dear New Healthcare Provider,

Welcome to this rewarding and challenging journey of providing care. As you begin working with patients, I encourage you to prioritize understanding their perspectives and meeting them where they are. This approach can greatly impact their sense of self-efficacy and commitment to their own health. 

I’ve seen firsthand how small changes, like taking a few extra moments to listen without interruption or asking about their daily challenges, can transform a patient's experience and foster trust. For example, I once had a patient who was hesitant to follow treatment recommendations due to her overwhelming responsibilities at home; by acknowledging her concerns and creating a flexible, personalized plan, we were able to work together to improve her health. 

Remember, being sensitive to the barriers your patients face and aligning your goals with theirs can empower them to take active roles in their care, ultimately leading to better outcomes. Your empathy, patience, and commitment to seeing the person behind the patient will make all the difference. 

Best of luck on your journey,  
Nauman Piracha MD

By seeing the world through the patients' eyes, providers can identify underlying factors that influence their behavior, such as cultural beliefs, personal values, or past experiences. This understanding fosters trust, improves communication, and enhances patient compliance with treatment plans. It also helps in addressing any fears or misconceptions patients may have, leading to more empathetic and respectful care that meets their unique needs and circumstances. Ultimately, it contributes to better health outcomes and a more positive patient experience.
ypTreatment1_2:
Understanding a patient's perspective can have a significant positive influence on both the patient and their recovery. When healthcare providers take the time to truly understand a patient’s feelings, beliefs, and motivations, it helps in building a strong therapeutic relationship based on trust and mutual respect. This connection can make patients feel heard, valued, and supported, reducing anxiety and increasing their willingness to engage in their treatment plan.

Additionally, understanding their perspective allows providers to tailor interventions that align with the patient’s values and lifestyle, making it more likely for them to adhere to the recommended treatments. It also enables healthcare providers to address any barriers or concerns the patient may have, such as fear of side effects or cultural hesitations, thus improving compliance. Overall, this approach not only enhances the patient’s emotional well-being but also promotes active participation in their own care, leading to improved recovery rates and better overall health outcomes.
ypTreatment2_1:
Patients may feel anxious or hesitant to ask questions for several reasons. Commonly, they might fear that their questions will seem silly or that they’ll be judged for not understanding medical jargon or complex information. Some patients worry about taking up too much of the healthcare provider’s time, especially if they perceive that the provider is busy or rushed. There can also be a power dynamic at play, where patients feel intimidated or uncomfortable challenging the authority of a healthcare professional.

Cultural factors may also contribute; in some cultures, questioning a doctor is considered disrespectful. Additionally, past negative experiences with healthcare providers, where patients felt dismissed or not listened to, can make them reluctant to speak up. Finally, anxiety or embarrassment about their health condition can make patients feel vulnerable, leading them to hold back on asking questions they genuinely want answers to. Understanding these reasons is crucial for healthcare providers to create a more open, supportive environment that encourages patient engagement and communication.

I began by asking open-ended questions about her life—her family, work, and what she enjoyed doing in her free time.

She shared stories about her children and her worries about being a burden to them. By listening without judgment and acknowledging her concerns, I was able to show her that I genuinely cared about her as an individual. This approach helped build trust, and over time, she became more comfortable sharing her fears and asking questions about her care. 

We worked together to develop a plan that accommodated her lifestyle, focusing on small, manageable steps rather than overwhelming changes. By centering the patient, getting to know her personally, and building trust, she felt more supported and empowered, which significantly improved her adherence to the treatment plan and ultimately her health outcomes. This experience reinforced the importance of truly seeing and hearing the patient beyond their medical condition.
