sayingTreatment:
Today, we explored the concept of delivering healthcare that truly prioritizes patients' perspectives and meets them where they are. This approach is not just about treating an illness, but about engaging with patients in a way that acknowledges their individual experiences and circumstances.

Research shows that when patients and physicians align on healthcare goals, patients feel more empowered and believe in their ability to manage their health. For instance, if a patient with diabetes and their doctor collaboratively set realistic goals, such as incorporating more fruits and vegetables into the diet rather than aiming for drastic lifestyle changes all at once, the patient is more likely to follow through. This concordance fosters a sense of self-efficacy, making patients feel more capable of managing their condition effectively.

I've seen firsthand how small changes in practice can significantly enhance patient trust. For example, one doctor I observed made it a point to ask open-ended questions during consultations and actively listened to the patient's responses before offering medical advice. This patient-centered approach not only made the patient feel heard but also helped build a stronger therapeutic alliance. The patient felt more comfortable discussing concerns and preferences, which led to more tailored and effective care.

Sensitivity to the barriers patients face on their health journey is crucial for fostering long-term well-being. Consider a situation where a patient struggles with adherence to a medication regimen due to side effects or financial constraints. A healthcare provider who acknowledges these challenges and works with the patient to find alternative solutions—such as exploring different medication options or connecting the patient with financial assistance resources—can significantly improve compliance and outcomes. By understanding and addressing these practical obstacles, healthcare providers empower patients to be more active participants in their care.

In summary, prioritizing patients' perspectives means engaging with them on their terms, setting shared goals, and addressing their unique challenges with empathy and practical solutions. This approach not only enhances trust and adherence but also contributes to better overall health outcomes.

manipCheckOpen_T: I read about how to best insure quality office visits with patients
sayingTreatment:
Welcome to our medical group.  We look forward to having you become an important member of our team and learning from one another.  We are focused on providing quality care to all our patients.  Your training program provided you with many of the clinical skills that you will rely upon and enhance throughout your career.  Our group has always emphasized the need provide patients with patient centered interactions that enhance the physician-patient relationship.  We have developed a "toolbox" to help achieve these goals that we refer to as the 4 E's: Engage, Empathize, Educate and Enlist.  

Engage: Taking the opportunity to connect with every patient at the outset of a visit.  A smile, a friendly comment, some physical contact such as a handshake or pat on the shoulder followed by always sitting down and avoiding focus on the electronic record.  Always asking for permission to look at the EHR briefly or enter data will assure the patient that they are your primary focus.

Empathy:  Expressions of empathy are among the most important interactions you will have with every patient. This skill requires practice for some physicians but will become second nature once fully adopted.  Patients will trust the recommendations you provide if they believe that you truly care about them.  If we interact with every patient as though they were a close family member, expressions of empathy will become more routine.

Educate:  Always talking to patients about their symptoms and concerns in non-medical terminology will make it more likely that they will understand what you are trying to say.  It's always best to never assume that a patient already knows what me mean when we use medical terms.  It never hurts to ask if he or she has any questions about what we expressed.

Enlist:  Developing a plan for the patient's care may seem like the physician's sole responsibility, but it only works when it is a collaborative process.  Asking "Does that sound like something you're willing to do?" is a great way to ensure that the patient will more likely follow it.

Following these simple routines will enhance the quality of your encounters with your patients.  This patient-centered approach will help provide you with a satisfying clinical experience throughout your medical career.

We look forward to working with you to achieve a successful career with our group.

Yours truly,
ypTreatment3_1: Every visit can be broken down into 4 categories: How the provider Engages the patient at the onset of the visit.  A warm greeting with a smile.  Sitting down facing the patient and not focusing on the electronic chart.  Beginning with a brief comment or question such as "How has your day been so far?" or "It's good to see you again.  I'm looking forward to catching up with you since our last visit."  Expressing Empathy early in the visit is also essential.  "I'm sorry to hear that your headaches are worse.  Let's see what we can do to help you reduce or eliminate them."  How you Educate the patient is also very important.  Using non-technical language to describe the problem and potential solutions is very important.  Explaining the diagnosis and underlying pathology in terms the patient can easily understand is essential.  Finally, Enlisting the patient in the plan going forward is an equally important part of a quality visit.  It's not "your plan" but a collaborative plan presented to the patient with the patient's consent and agreement.  It does no good for the provider to add a medication or recommend a diet or exercise program if the patient doesn't agree.  In summary, a good visit is made up of the 4 Es:  Engage, Empathize, Educate and Enlist.
ypTreatment4: A middle aged Asian man who was raising 2 sons on his own due to his wife's demise several years earlier had been my patient for 5 years.  His sons were in their late teens and the older son had expressed interest in a career in medicine.  The older son spent a summer during his second year of college shadowing me in my office and learning more about becoming a physician.  He was later accepted to Stanford medical school and became an interventional radiologist.  His younger brother became increasingly depressed and withdrawn with his school grades beginning to suffer.  His father, my patient, expressed his concern for his younger son's future and depressed state.  I asked to have the younger son make an appointment with me.  I learned that the younger son was most interested in computer gaming and was very skilled and savvy about writing computer software.  I urged him to pursue a career in writing software for computer games.  Over the course of several years working with a software gaming company he became an executive with the company and was earning more than his older brother.  All is well that ends well.  Listening to the patient and learning what might help reduce his anxiety was the key to his success.

I picked altruism as one of my values because it is the primary reason I chose healthcare as a profession. sayingTreatment: Welcome to the world of medicine. The profession you have chosen is more sacred than is probably advertised in this day in age and their will be days where you feel like everyone is against you, you’ve made no difference, and that patient expectations are ridiculous and out of touch with the reality of science and medicine. However, you must always remember that people are often negative and hostile out of fear and inability to understand, and any challenges you face when dealing with these types of emotions and people is best done with grace and safe guarding of your heart. As long as you practice with the balance of “doing no harm” to your patients, but also standing firm on your “expertise and understanding of science, medicine, and the human body”, you will be ok. sayingTreatment:

I hope that you meet people where they are, because if you don't, then even the most well-intentioned patients may struggle to follow your treatment plan to the letter.

I hope that you listen. Because even when you're having a busy or bad day in the office or in the hospital, the person sitting across from you is there because they're having a worse day.

sayingTreatment:
As a provider you will have rules/regulations to comply by and limited resources and time at your disposal. You will have to carefully decide which patients will receive more of your time, efforts, and dedication. More complicated medical conditions or patients with communication/socio-economic barriers, in my experience, warrant going the extra mile for your patients. 

Additionally, you learn how to manage your finances, build your practice, learn about taxation, etc. These subjects, for some reason, are viewed as taboo in medical school and residency and avoided by administration.

If I don't address their concerns of costs and and side effects first, they will likely not even take the medications I prescribe and thus not treat the disease. ypTreatment3_1:
I find the relationship to be fundamental to anything that I am doing as a physician.
I try to being each visit with non-medical conversation to help establish a bond.  For patients from another culture, I often try to show some familiarity with their culture (food or traditions) or if unfamiliar to inquire about their culture and show curiosity in their lives and families. When moving on the medical part of the visit, I try to always ask their opinion on what they would like to do after explaining what I think and what the options may be.
ypTreatment4: I have an elderly patient who has multiple medical problems.   She loves to read and I always ask about what she is currently reading.
